name: Dana Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Dana, 43, and I help the senior electrician wire and repair homes and shops, often before the shops open. I've got a vocational certificate, but I'm still junior, slower and less skilled than the others, with my work checked. Our firm pays above the usual rate, including the early starts; my partner repairs shoes, and years of saving have left us with eight months of expenses put aside. We've got children aged six and twelve and a mortgage, and I use AI now and then for a short customer update after a colleague showed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, then we can stop treating every new booking message like a sign from the future. I use AI now and then to tidy a customer update after a colleague showed me, and that's enough. I'd still want the right drill bit when the shopkeeper lets us in at six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our mortgage and bills are covered, and we've got eight months of expenses saved. I'm still junior, but this firm pays above the usual rate, including the early starts, and there are plenty of other firms nearby. In that picture I can learn without thinking every mistake means the family loses its income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep helping with early shop installations and supervised home repairs. Starting this week I'd check the next morning's tools against the senior electrician's list before leaving the yard. Through the first year I'd keep doing that and asking about anything I didn't understand rather than buying a new tool just to feel current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with enough room to admit I'm still learning. I don't love making a second trip to the van because I've brought the wrong size fitting. I like knowing an ordinary mistake can be corrected without the whole week becoming a financial crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you become a junior electrician at 43?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worked in a family furniture shop before taking a vocational certificate to change direction. I'm still below the others for speed and practical skill, and the senior checks my work. The household cushion came from years of saving, not from being secretly brilliant at this new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who shares that household plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner repairs shoes, and we have children aged six and twelve and a mortgage. We both put money aside when we could. Eight months saved doesn't mean we want to live on it, but it makes learning a trade less frightening.

say: I'd keep occasional **customer-update tools** without treating every booking message as a prediction.
I'd rather arrive with the **right tools** for an early shop visit.
think: Our **mortgage and bills** are covered, with eight months of expenses saved.
The firm's **higher pay** and plenty of nearby employers let me learn without fearing every mistake costs our living.
do: Keep helping with **shop installations** and supervised home repairs through the first year.
Check **next morning's tools** against the senior electrician's list before leaving the yard, starting now.
feel: **Calm**, with enough financial room to acknowledge mistakes and continue practical learning.
S0.quote: The household cushion came from years of saving, not from being secretly brilliant at this new job.
fieldNote: Her **strong cushion** comes from prior household saving and higher current pay, while vocational training and below-average practical skill remain explicit.
Her **occasional AI use** follows a colleague's demonstration and stays separate from supervised work and the familiar tool-list habit.

steps.text: Keep supervised electrical jobs and check tomorrow's tools against the senior's list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say quicker booking could be a help, but the office staff deserve to know what's happening before the new system turns up. I'd try a proven tool after somebody had shown me the result. I wouldn't tell a customer we could finish earlier just because the diary looked tidier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own paid days to stay steady because the company still needs the same physical crew on its booked installations. Our reserve and the other employers nearby give me more room than some people have. I'm uneasy about the office jobs changing first and about promises being made without the people doing the work in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the senior this month to show me the approved AI booking-update tool on one completed week after the office had tested it. If the details matched the actual visits, I'd learn to use the update screen with each draft checked before it went out. During the first year I'd keep my physical role and flag any appointment that didn't leave enough time for the agreed work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how the change reaches people, rather than scared about my next wage. I'm comfortable being a later user once something has been tested. I'd rather ask twice than promise a shopkeeper an impossible opening time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in the completed week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The address, the work agreed and whether the visit left time for the checks the senior required. I'd ask about anything the update changed. I'm not qualified to shorten a repair by clicking a different box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you expect your own job to disappear in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not over the next few years with the physical work we've booked. I'd revise that if the actual diary emptied or paid days changed. I don't want my confidence to become an answer that ignores new facts.

say: I'd want **office staff** told what is happening before a booking system arrives.
I'd test a proven **update tool** without promising repairs finish faster because the diary looks tidy.
think: I expect my **paid days** to hold while booked installations still need the same physical crew.
I'm uneasy about **office changes** and decisions made without the people doing the work.
do: Request a **demonstration** this month after the office has tested the approved AI tool on a completed week.
Learn the **update screen** only if details match actual visits, checking drafts before sending them.
Keep **physical work** during the first year and flag appointments that leave insufficient time.
feel: **Uneasy** about colleagues and promises, with her own near-term wage feeling secure.
S1.quote: I'm not qualified to shorten a repair by clicking a different box.
fieldNote: Her **own-income confidence** rests on booked physical installations, while her concern remains with office staff and the handling of change.
She retains **steady adoption** through prior office testing, a completed-week demonstration and checked drafts rather than immediate unsupported use.

steps.text: Learn the AI booking-update screen after office testing and a checked completed-week demonstration
Keep physical repair work and flag appointments without enough checking time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner the first date is thinking AI in 2028, with capable robots around 2031. I'd say those three years still matter, but not because people with tools are safe forever. I'd ask the senior what our actual paid work might be through the first stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose hours as a junior when robots start doing the simple physical tasks I help with. Eight months saved gives me time to choose, but our children and mortgage don't disappear when a company buys a machine. I don't know whether all the nearby firms would keep taking juniors together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask this month for the supervisor's actual view of confirmed paid work, marking anything uncertain as uncertain. I'd also check posted helper vacancies monthly without resigning. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid supervised work and apply elsewhere only for stated pay and paid hours that met our household costs, comparing a written offer before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, but not pushed into the first offer. I can tell the family we've got some breathing room without claiming the reserve lasts forever. I'd rather use the cash to choose carefully than buy a course out of fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a new helper job worth considering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The actual tasks, what supervision was provided, the paid hours and travel costs as well as the wage. A new company name doesn't prove the work is safer from robots. I'd want a written offer that fitted our numbers before handing in notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you draw on savings to accept lower pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as a permanent way to make a wage look enough. We could use the reserve during a short gap, but a job still has to cover the ordinary household budget. I'd talk that through with my partner before agreeing anything.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from robots around 2031 without calling physical work permanently safe.
I'd ask about **actual paid work** through the first stage rather than rely on a reassuring date.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink when robots do simple physical tasks.
Eight months saved provides **choice time**, while nearby firms may face the same changes and cannot all be assumed to hire.
do: Ask now about **confirmed paid work**, marking uncertainty rather than counting hoped-for shifts.
Check posted **helper vacancies** monthly while retaining my current job.
Apply after **2028** only for adequate stated pay and paid hours, comparing supervision, travel and a written offer before leaving.
feel: **Anxious** about own earnings, with resources to avoid a rushed offer or fear-driven course purchase.
S2.quote: A new company name doesn't prove the work is safer from robots.
fieldNote: She makes **conditional job searches** rather than assuming plentiful local employers remain independent shelters from the same robot capability.
The **offer conditions** include adequate pay, paid hours, supervision and travel costs; existing reserves are not treated as permanent wage subsidies.

steps.text: Keep paid supervised electrical work after 2028 while checking confirmed days
Seek posted supervised roles after 2028 with written pay and hours covering household costs after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to check a course and then use the teaching, rather than collect certificates in a panic. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I'd still want the children to understand that learning is useful without being a promise that one job lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own income looks secure over the next few years, and I can afford a modest practical course without touching the emergency reserve. I'd be 48 when thinking AI arrived, so I still need a working plan for years after that. I'm uneasy about the later competition, not expecting our household income to collapse next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the senior about the 240 weekend drawing class a former apprentice recommended. I'd enrol next term only after checking the teaching fitted our jobs, paying the fee from spare earnings with no lost paid shifts and childcare agreed with my partner. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep supervised repairs and use the completed class only on routes the senior still checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I like having time to do an ordinary thing properly. A recommendation from somebody who finished the course is worth more to me than a bright advert. I'd still want to see whether the teaching improved my actual work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the dates clashed with work or your partner's hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for another class rather than quietly assume the children would manage. We've got room to choose, which is a reason not to rush. I wouldn't pay the fee until we had a workable date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the course make you independent of supervision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still have a vocational certificate and the same limits unless I earned a different qualification and the employer authorised different work. I'd ask the senior to compare how I explained a route before and after the course. I'd want fewer corrections, not a new title on a badge.

say: I'd use **five years** to check practical teaching and apply it rather than collect panic certificates.
I'd explain that **learning** can help without guaranteeing one job lasts forever.
think: My **near-term income** looks secure, and a modest course can come from spare earnings rather than emergency savings.
At **48** in 2031, I'll still need a working plan beyond the first AI date.
do: Check the recommended **240 drawing class** with the senior this month.
Enrol only with **useful teaching**, spare-earnings funding, no lost paid shifts and agreed childcare.
Keep **supervised repairs** after 2031 and use completed teaching only on senior-checked routes.
feel: **Uneasy** about later competition, with patience to select and assess a practical course.
S3.quote: I'd want fewer corrections, not a new title on a badge.
fieldNote: Her **self-funded class** is affordable but still depends on useful content, spare earnings, protected paid shifts and actual childcare agreement.
She explicitly retains **junior authority** after the course, using observed corrections rather than assuming a new qualification or independent sign-off rights.

steps.text: Take useful 240 drawing class from spare earnings only with paid shifts protected and childcare agreed
Keep supervised repairs after 2031 on senior-checked routes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to plan sensibly without chasing every new tool. I'd keep learning useful practical things and checking the family's real costs. I'd tell the children to ask good questions about training, rather than choose a life from a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our current earnings and eight-month reserve to keep the next few years secure. Thinking AI in 2036 would find me at 53, with robots around age 56, so I won't assume I can retire out of the problem. I'm uneasy about the longer future, but I don't feel that every bill this year is under threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue our normal monthly saving now and take the same 240 class only if the teaching fitted, the fee came from spare earnings, work pay was protected and childcare was agreed. Each year my partner and I would review actual paid days, mortgage costs and the reserve. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid work and compare any new offer with real household costs before deciding to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy when I think far ahead, but comfortable about how we're managing now. I like the longer warning because I can make decisions in order. I don't have to call every ordinary family weekend a missed chance to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the annual review change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid days staying down for a couple of months, or the reserve being used for normal bills instead of a one-off repair. We'd look at actual figures rather than wait for a big announcement. I'd talk to the supervisor about the work and my partner about what we could change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your older child about choosing training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ask what you will actually learn, who teaches it and what the cost means for you. A course brochure isn't the same as a paid job at the end. I'd help my child ask, not pretend I can remove all uncertainty by naming the right trade.

say: I'd use **ten years** for ordered decisions rather than chase every tool or headline.
I'd encourage the **children** to question training claims and compare them with actual costs.
think: Current **earnings and reserves** make the next few years secure for our household.
I remain **uneasy** about later competition and cannot assume retirement at the thinking-AI or robot dates.
do: Continue **normal saving** now and take the class only within the same funding, pay and childcare conditions.
Review **paid days** and mortgage costs with my partner yearly, checking reserve use.
Keep **paid work** after 2036 and compare offers with actual household costs before leaving.
feel: **Uneasy** about the longer future, with present finances comfortable enough to enjoy ordinary family time.
S4.quote: A course brochure isn't the same as a paid job at the end.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** keeps her own near-term security separate from later uncertainty, without assuming pension access or a cleared mortgage.
The **annual review** names observable income and reserve changes, while course costs, wage protection and childcare consent remain material conditions.

steps.text: Continue ordinary saving from current wages
Take useful 240 drawing class from spare earnings only with paid shifts protected and childcare agreed
Keep paid work after 2036 and compare new offers against actual household costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots follow around 2031 while I'm still learning the simpler physical tasks. Clear paid-hour offers and patient practical teaching would help. I'd rather have a usable route to keep earning than buy a course because somebody made me feel late.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the worker is actually allowed to do after the course. My children need the wage from my real job, not the job printed on a course advert. I want to get better without pretending the certificate gives me skills I haven't practised.

headlineQuote: My children need the wage from my real job, not the job printed on a course advert.
portrait: Dana is **43**, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, below-average practical speed and senior checks despite higher pay for her work.
Her **partner repairs shoes**, with two school-age children, a mortgage, eight months saved and plenty of nearby electrical employers.
She uses **AI occasionally** after demonstration, preferring proven examples and clear limits to rushed adoption.
Short timelines prompt **written-offer comparisons**; longer ones permit a checked course from spare earnings without lost wages or unagreed childcare.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less learning time before robots around 2031 could reduce her junior physical-work hours.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **paid-hour offers** and patient practical teaching would support continued earning.
A **usable course route** would help more than fear-driven buying or claims of skills she has not practised.
